fixability.reason: additive index, zero behaviour risk (payment is read on amount, paid_date and no existing index leads with those columns)

candidates.description: Create a non-unique index on payment(paid_date) to allow the WHERE filter to use an index instead of a full table scan.
candidates.predicted_effect: rows examined drop from ~19,911,200 to ~50 per request
what_could_break: If the database already has a conflicting index name, migration will fail.
MySQL may choose not to use the index if the query planner deems a full scan cheaper for very low selectivity.

schema_proof.column_rationale: paid_date leads the index because it is filtered by equality in this statement's own WHERE clause, in the order the predicate names them — a composite index can only use its leading columns for an equality seek, so a range or sort column has to come after them, never before.

candidates.description: Rewrite the JPQL query to a native SQL query that explicitly forces the use of the newly added paid_date index via a USE INDEX hint, eliminating the full scan.
candidates.predicted_effect: rows examined drop from ~19,911,200 to ~50 per request
candidates.sql_before: SELECT `p1_0`.`id`, `p1_0`.`invoice_id`, `p1_0`.`amount`, `p1_0`.`paid_date` FROM `payment` `p1_0` WHERE `p1_0`.`paid_date` = ? ORDER BY `p1_0`.`id` LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
candidates.sql_after: SELECT `p1_0`.`id`, `p1_0`.`invoice_id`, `p1_0`.`amount`, `p1_0`.`paid_date` FROM `payment` AS `p1_0` USE INDEX (idx_payment_paid_date) WHERE `p1_0`.`paid_date` = ? ORDER BY `p1_0`.`id` LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
what_could_break: Native query bypasses JPA mapping; mismatched column aliases could cause mapping errors.
If the index name changes or is not present, the USE INDEX hint will be ignored.
